en: And may my elder Kül fall into my hands!
Let me overthrow the hero and find peace;
To learn what is to come,
Let me cast the divining lots now.
If in his old age God shows Khan Bakai
The prince once more,
If in Kanykei's old age
God shows me my mother,
Whose days have passed in lamentation—
There is snow upon its mountains,
Game within its forests,
Deer among its broken hills,
Wild sheep upon its hills,
Ibex upon its terraces,
Kulan on its pale plains,
Silver on its sunny slopes;
Its springs flow in abundance,
Its nightingales sing sweetly,
And a grieving person finds relief.
The tops of its willows bend,
Lines are drawn across its sands,
The gold within its earth is revealed—
May God show me my settled Keng-Kol,
My broad land of Talas!
If the time comes for him to grant it,
If fortune and happiness fill my path,
If God sets what lies behind us right,
I shall lower my spear
Against the wrestler who challenges me;
Making the spear my divining token,
I shall cry out and strike
The great wrestler Küzhürmön.
God, hear my tears;
If you do not wither my head,
Let me cast a sure divination.
Making my own head the stake,
I shall spear Küzhürmön.
If I chance to spear Küzhürmön,
If by chance I hurl him down,
My work and fortune will prosper;
The sister-in-law I take as my support
Will bear a son.
If I am thrown and fall from my horse,
If Küzhürmön spears and strikes me,
Then let me read that omen:
Rather than be called a captive slave,
If Küzhürmön casts me down,
Let me die before my appointed death.
Let this wretched life behold
The true place from which none return!
Küzhürmön, who came out to joust,
Was a lion full of courage,
Merciless, unmatched on foot,
And a master upon a horse.
He never fled from fire or attack,
And thrust his spear from afar;
Formidable wrestler Küzhürmön
Had won in many contests.
In wrestling he spared no wrestler;
One young horse nursed by a barren mare
Could not satisfy him for a single meal.
When Küzhürmön became aroused,
Many men trembled,
Lost their senses and stood still,
Their two eyes widening.
He was a terror surpassing the world;
Whoever approached him stopped.
Taking a spear with a steel shaft,
This villain had long prepared
To shed blood—
Such was Küzhürmön's nature.
When unbeliever and Muslim
Clashed in battle,
He performed dreadful deeds.
When a Chinese giant ravaged
And slaughtered the Kyrgyz people,
Riding a black rhinoceros,
The dark, stubborn champion on foot
Had come out in single combat;
The hero Küzhürmön
Thrust his spear in that duel,
Toppled the black, stubborn warrior
From the back of his rhinoceros,
And cut off his head.
The khan and all the people marveled:
“Küzhürmön is this mighty;
He has destroyed the giant he fought
And driven that terror into the earth.
He is both a hero and a lion;
Among all sons of men who took up spears,
He long ago surpassed them all.
He buried every sworn enemy
In the earth without digging a grave;
He is the mightiest among the people.”
Against enemies in bitter combat
He had caused many a conflict.
Of your elder Külchoro the slave,
Küzhürmön had cut open
Both rows of his shoulder blades,
Breaking through the forest to make a road;
He humiliated my elder,
Külchoro, lion among men,
Opening those wounds,
Inflicting calamity,
Dealing him humiliation,
And beginning his violence.
If one keeps telling it, it never ends;
There is still much in the unfinished tale.
But the young hero Karadöö
Was there to joust with him.
Beyond lay Keng-Sai and Alai;
The Karadöö you see
Held much within his heart:
If the spear cast as an omen
Found its proper chance, he would
Offer Küzhürmön as a sacrifice,
Drive his spear in to the shaft,
And plunge it wherever he faced.
His insides had long burned with misery
To avenge Külchoro;
Such was the poor man's state.
Taking the contest as his omen,
Karadöö's heroic heart was troubled;
Tears flowed down both cheeks
And poured over his collarbones.
He looked at nothing around him,
Gave no thought to his own death;
Taking up the spear without concern,
He counted Kyyaz's massed host
As less than the hem of his garment.
He wore a gray brocade coat
And rode a gray Badam horse;
He adorned and tightly knotted
The tail of his swift mount.
Like a molting vulture he glowered,
Like a crouching tiger he advanced.
When Küzhürmön entered the contest,
The sight dismayed the heart;
His build and great size
Looked like a gray hill.
He sprang like a tiger;
None who fought him would survive.
He charged like a wild boar,
Tore like a wolf,
And lumbered like a bear.
Küzhürmön came to strike with his spear
Before one could even cry, “Speak!”
He could sling anyone he met
Across his saddle and descend the ridge;
If anyone turned aside,
He could catch him even at a furious gallop.
Enraged, he seemed to pursue the fleeing;
Küzhürmön would seize and crush
Anyone who opposed him.
His face was hard as iron,
His exertion solid as a cliff;
His surging seemed to shake the world,
As though he would swallow anyone who turned.
He seemed able to win
The offered prize without a word.
Küzhürmön had come;
Huge and well matched to a hero,
He entered the spear contest that time,
And possessed immense strength.
He had jostled the whole world;
In contests with the spear,
The madman had won every prize
Without letting anyone utter a sound.
He held sway over Zheti-Özön.
He began the struggle fiercely;
Whenever he met a sworn enemy,
That hulking, brutish slave
Tore him limb from limb.
All who saw his figure marveled.
His spear was wound with brass;
Whoever fought him collapsed.
Many wrestlers, encountering Küzhürmön,
Had crawled away.
From among the people Küzhürmön
Whipped on his Badam horse,
Taking a pine-like spear;
Enraged and fully prepared,
Onto the marked bank and stony field
He burst into the contest,
Making his accursed champion steed
Rear and surge beneath him.
If you ask about Karadöö,
He was still somewhat childish and awkward,
Still unseasoned in every speech.
Leaning against the gray mountain ridge,
Wrapped in gray-mottled dust,
He had never before competed for a prize,
Never speared a man face to face,
And had not yet won fame among the people.
The hardy warhorse,
With sieve-like lungs and copper forelegs,
The gray five-year-old fit for battle,
Had been trained from birth
And kept for Karadöö,
For it was a true champion steed.
Its parrot-like tail streamed behind;
The brass-beaked spirit woman
Had tested and recognized it
As an unfailing racer.
Many judges and skilled experts
Had it raised unseen by the people.
At its birth Khan Koshoy,
The aged father of the people,
The saint who outlived generations,
Saw and approved it.
Bilerik came from afar
And repeatedly asked for it.
The gray-maned sultan Semetey
Would not give it when asked:
“Let this gray horse of Kambar-Ata
Run among the herds;
If hardship comes upon us,
If a precious life is hard pressed,
Unknown Karadöö,
My falcon, shall ride it.
He will be my heir;
Karadöö will mourn and weep for me,
And grieve when I am gone.
It is a falcon no man should see,
A steed surpassing many others.
Its back is high and its belly low;
Wherever one rides it, it never tires.
Holding its reins never wearies the hand.
If a stallion charges into battle,
It will not surrender its rider to the foe.
It must be kin to the kulan-chasing
Karager of old Kaiyp,
Zhoruger of the raider,
And Er Töshtük's Chalkuiruk.
It must be kin to all of those.
It is a perfect, peerless steed;
Those four princely horses are one kin,
Children of the wind-spirit.”
Encountered in the unseen,
White-bearded old Kydyr,
From old Kydyr's hands,
From beyond Arabanty and Buura,
Below those places,
Beyond Andizhan
And this side of Marghilan,
The madcap, while still a foal,
Had been found for Külchoro.
Its tail streamed even as a yearling;
Knowing it would be an heir in hard times,
Your wise mother Kanykei,
That discerning woman, had tested it.
She had it covered carefully with a blanket
And raised out of the people's sight.
Such was the gray five-year-old's story.
When the gray-maned hero vanished,
Kanchoro seized Külchoro
